extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, poetics, and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing or evaluating classical/Aristotelian tragedy: its aims, formal features (action, unity, magnitude), emotional effects (pity, fear, katharsis), use of language and music, and the moral/aesthetic balance of characters and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustriousness/quality of principal actors
rubrics_metrics.description: “the action which affords matter for an Epic poem be illustrious and important in itself; ... it must be so by the quality of the persons who act.” Aristotle holds that the chief actors in tragedy ought to be illustrious by birth and position; moral nobility is demanded rather than mere outward rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The status, reputation, or moral nobility of characters supplies grandeur and credibility to the action: eminent persons' greatness makes the action great and credible. Note the caution that critics have sometimes confused moral nobility with mere courtly dignity or outward rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary end of poetry — refined pleasure (delight)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the end of poetry is a refined pleasure... If the poet fails to produce the proper pleasure, he fails in the specific function of his art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry's chief aim is to give delight (dulce) rather than to instruct (utile); instruction may be admitted secondarily. A work may be morally useful yet fail as poetry if it does not produce aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's definition: tragedy is “an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seriousness = not ludicrous or morally trivial (grave/great); completeness = a whole, unified action with beginning, middle, end; magnitude (μέγεθος) has been variously read — it can mean intrinsic greatness/significance of action and can also (mis)be taken to refer to length or duration. Beware conflating these senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and embellishment: several kinds of artistic ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is in “language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ‘several kinds of embellishment’ are verse and song: verse (without music) in dialogue and lyrical song in the choral parts. Different embellishments should be distributed to appropriate sections of the drama; the choice of language/meter contributes to tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form: dramatic imitation of action, not narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is “in the form of action, not of narrative.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work must present the action by enactment (mimesis) rather than recounting events; the experience of the spectator through performed action is essential to tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity and fear to effect katharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must act “through pity and fear effecting the proper katharsis, or ‘purgation, of these emotions.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The play's proper function is to arouse the specific aesthetic emotions of pity and fear and to bring about their appropriate purgation/relief (katharsis). Different commentators debate what katharsis fully means, but the evocation of these two emotions is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of katharsis — purgation/clarification of morbid elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Katharsis carries a medical metaphor: it denotes either expulsion of a disturbing element (removal) or purification/clarification of the person/feelings subjected to the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations include: (a) a medical/homoeopathic model (tragedy excites pity and fear to provide pleasurable relief), (b) a purgation of the morbid or excessive element in those emotions so that feeling becomes clarified. The Politics passage and musical examples indicate katharsis as a kind of regulated emotional discharge with aesthetic satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise character of pity and fear to be invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear: “a species of pain or disturbance arising from an impression of impending evil which is destructive or painful in its nature.” Pity: “a sort of pain at an evident evil of a destructive or painful kind in the case of somebody who does not deserve it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pity is felt for the undeserving sufferer (often when the suffering seems near), and fear arises from witnessing a similar fate that might befall ourselves; in tragedy these feelings are correlated and modified by imaginative distance and identification with the hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification: the tragic hero must be like us (ὅμοιος)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The tragic sufferer is a man like ourselves (ὅμοιος);” the hero's moral resemblance to the audience is crucial to enlist sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close moral likeness (not identical perfection) permits the audience to feel fear and pity. The hero's similarity arouses identification and makes tragic emotions effective; dramatic construction should foreground relatable moral traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character complexity: hero neither flawless nor monstrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's hero is “not a man of flawless perfection, nor yet one of consummate villainy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic protagonist should possess sufficient virtue or resemblance to the audience to provoke pity and fear, but also contain a flaw or error that leads to downfall; avoid extremes (perfect saint or absolute villain) so that the suffering appears undeserved yet plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music as a distinct vehicle for katharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes musical katharsis: impassioned melodies can perform a kathartic (homoeopathic) cure, distinct from music used for moral education, relaxation, or higher aesthetic enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use impassioned choral music (μίμησίς τις of the enthusiasm) to provide an outlet for emotional excess; recognize multiple musical functions and select musical modes that produce the intended cathartic effect, especially in choral passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute moral instruction for aesthetic end
rubrics_metrics.description: Although aesthetic representation is viewed under ethical lights, “he never allows the moral purpose of the poet or the moral effects of his art to take the place of the artistic end.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the primacy of aesthetic pleasure/delight: ethical teaching may be present but must not replace the requirement that the work satisfy its artistic function. A poem that instructs but does not delight is a failure as poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as a portrayal of human destiny/well‑being (eudaimonia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is concerned with a serious end, namely eudaimonia — that well‑being which is the true end of life; it is a picture of human destiny in all its significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The action should address matters of human flourishing, fate, or the fundamental goods/ills of life so that the stakes feel weighty and universal rather than trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reputation to render action credible and magnificent
rubrics_metrics.description: “The greatness of these eminent men renders the action great, and their reputation makes it credible and possible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leveraging character reputation and social standing can confer grandeur on the plot and make otherwise improbable actions acceptable to the audience; reputation can be a structural device to elevate ordinary actions to tragic importance.
